opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a great question, and one I think about a lot, because there's a real tension in the field right now.

On one side, we've got these remarkable pretrained models. They've absorbed an enormous amount of human-generated data, and they carry a lot of useful structure: language, common patterns about the world, ways of describing things. On the other side, there's the perspective I come from, the reinforcement learning, Alberta-style view, where intelligence comes from an agent interacting with its world, making predictions, taking actions, seeing what happens, and continually updating from that stream of experience.

I don't think those two things are necessarily at odds, but I do think we need to be careful about which one is in the driver's seat. A pretrained model is a snapshot. It's a fixed record of what people have said and done up to some point. That's valuable, the way a library is valuable. But an agent that lives in the world, and I think a lot about this from our work on prosthetic limbs, is facing a situation that's changing all the time. The person's body changes, the environment changes, their goals change throughout the day. No amount of pretraining fully anticipates the specifics of that one person's life.

So the way I'd frame it is that foundation models can be a very good starting point, a prior, a source of useful features or representations, or even a kind of advisor the agent can consult. But the real learning, the part that makes the system truly yours and truly adaptive, has to come from the agent's own ongoing experience. It has to be able to form its own predictions about its own sensorimotor stream, test them, and revise them.

There are also some real technical challenges in making that marriage work. Big pretrained networks aren't naturally built for continual learning. We see things like loss of plasticity, where networks trained for a long time get worse at learning new things, and catastrophic forgetting, where new learning overwrites old learning. If we just bolt a frozen foundation model onto an agent, we may get a nice head start but lose the ability to keep growing. So a lot of the interesting research now is about how you take that pretrained knowledge and keep it plastic, keep it open to being reshaped by experience.

Ultimately, my bet is that the most capable and most helpful systems will be the ones where experience is the primary teacher and the pretrained knowledge serves the agent, rather than the other way around. Human knowledge is a gift we can give these systems, but they still have to grow up in the world themselves.

r002.rationale: It presents foundation models as a useful starting point or source of representations while saying the agent’s ongoing experience drives its learning.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because there's a temptation to treat these as competing paradigms, and I really don't see it that way.

The way I'd frame it is that a pretrained foundation model is a very good starting point. It's a compressed summary of an enormous amount of human experience, and that's genuinely valuable. If I'm building an agent that has to operate in the world, I'd be foolish not to take advantage of that. It gives the agent priors, it gives it language, it gives it a rough sense of how things tend to work.

But a starting point is not the same as learning. The thing that matters to me, and this goes back to the work we've done on continual learning and on agents that are embedded in a stream of experience, is what happens after deployment. The agent is interacting with a particular environment, a particular person, a particular prosthetic limb and a particular user's body, in our case. None of that was in the pretraining data. The specifics of that interaction only become available once the agent is actually there, acting and observing the consequences.

So the question I'd ask of any system is: what does it do with the next observation? If the answer is nothing, if the model is frozen and it just emits actions from a fixed set of weights, then I'd say it's a very capable tool, but it's not really learning from its own experience. Whereas if the agent can take what the foundation model gives it and then continue to update, to build predictions about its own stream of sensations and rewards, to notice when the world is different from what it expected, that's where I get excited.

I'd also push back a bit on the idea that the foundation model should be the center of the agent. I think it's more natural to see it as one component, one source of knowledge the agent can draw on, alongside the knowledge it's building from its own interaction. In the prosthetics work, for example, the thing that makes the difference for a person is that the device adapts to them, over days and weeks. A general model can't know that person. It can give you a good first guess, and then the real learning begins.

So, short version: foundation models are a wonderful prior and a terrible excuse to stop learning. The interesting science is in the interface between the two.

r002.rationale: It describes using a foundation model as a starting point while continuing to update from the agent’s own interactions and observations.

r003.rationale: It calls the interface between foundation models and ongoing learning interesting science, but does not say that learning models directly from raw agent experience is comparatively underexplored.

astra-6.text:
I see them as complementary. A pretrained foundation model gives an agent a rich starting point—structure and knowledge drawn from a tremendous amount of other people’s experience. The interesting question is how the agent connects that starting point to its own stream of interaction: what it observes, what it does, and what happens as a consequence.

For an agent interacting with a person, that matters because general knowledge only takes you so far. The agent needs to learn about this particular person, in this particular situation. What are they trying to accomplish? How does their behaviour change over time? And are the agent’s actions actually helping?

So I wouldn’t see pretraining as the end of learning. I’d see it as something that can make learning from experience more effective. The agent still needs to make predictions, test those predictions through interaction, and adapt when its expectations don’t match what happens. That ongoing relationship between knowledge and experience is where a lot of the opportunity lies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re complementary. A pretrained model gives an agent a rich starting point—structure that’s been learned from a great deal of other experience. But there’s still a question of what that knowledge means for this agent, with its particular sensors, its particular actions, and the things it’s trying to accomplish.

That’s where learning from its own experience becomes essential. If I take this action, what happens next? Can I predict the consequences, and can I use those predictions to make better decisions? A foundation model can help with that, but the agent needs to be able to test its expectations against the world and adapt when they’re wrong.

So I wouldn’t view pretraining as the end of learning. I’d view it as something that can make ongoing learning more effective. The interesting challenge is connecting that broad prior knowledge to a system that keeps learning through interaction.
